title: What personnel training does the Seveso III Directive require at major hazard sites?
description: What Seveso III (Directive 2012/18/EU) Annex III requires for identifying and providing training in a major hazard site's safety management system.
shortAnswer: The Seveso III Directive (Directive 2012/18/EU) requires operators of establishments holding dangerous substances above set thresholds to run a safety management system that, under Annex III, defines the roles of personnel involved in managing major hazards, identifies their training needs, provides that training, and involves employees and relevant subcontractors. It also requires specific emergency training for all personnel working in the establishment, including relevant subcontracted personnel, with internal emergency plans tested at least every three years.
keyTakeaways: Annex III, point (b)(i) of Directive 2012/18/EU requires the safety management system to identify the training needs of personnel involved in managing major hazards and to provide that training.
Annex III, point (b)(v) requires specific emergency training for all personnel working in the establishment, including relevant subcontracted personnel.
Upper tier establishments must have a safety report demonstrating the safety management system and an internal emergency plan reviewed and tested at intervals of no longer than three years.

The major accident prevention policy must be reviewed at least every five years, and inspections must take place at least yearly for upper tier and every three years for lower tier sites unless a systematic appraisal sets another program.
The directive has applied since June 1, 2015 and replaced Seveso II (Directive 96/82/EC).
jurisdiction: European Union (applied through each Member State's national law)
regulator: National Seveso competent authorities designated by each Member State, which inspect establishments; the European Commission monitors implementation
appliesTo: Operators of lower tier and upper tier establishments where dangerous substances are present at or above Annex I thresholds
Personnel involved in the management of major hazards at all levels of the organization
All personnel working in the establishment, for emergency training
Subcontracted personnel important to safety, including long term subcontractors

sections.heading: What is the Seveso III Directive and which sites does it cover?

blocks.text: Seveso III is [Directive 2012/18/EU](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32012L0018) of July 4, 2012 on the control of major accident hazards involving dangerous substances. It is the European Union's law for preventing major accidents at industrial sites and limiting their consequences for human health and the environment. Article 31 required Member States to transpose it by May 31, 2015 and apply it from June 1, 2015, and Article 32 repealed Seveso II, Directive 96/82/EC, from the same date.

Coverage depends on the quantity of dangerous substances present. Article 3 defines a lower tier establishment as one where dangerous substances are present at or above the Column 2 quantities of Annex I but below Column 3, and an upper tier establishment as one at or above Column 3, applying the summation rule where relevant. Article 2(2) excludes, among others, military establishments, hazards from ionizing radiation, transport of dangerous substances outside establishments, pipelines, mines and quarries, offshore exploration, and waste landfill sites, with specific exceptions such as onshore underground gas storage and tailings facilities.

Unlike the occupational safety directives covered elsewhere in this library, such as the [OSH Framework Directive](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training), Seveso III is primarily an industrial accident and environmental protection law. Worker training duties under the occupational safety directives continue to apply at the same site. As at November 2026, the directive has not been amended since adoption. According to the [European Commission](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/industrial-emissions-and-safety/industrial-accidents_en), it entered into force on August 13, 2012, applies to over 11,000 industrial installations across the EU, and was the subject of a second implementation report released on September 19, 2025.

sections.heading: What does Annex III require for organization and personnel training?

blocks.text: Annex III, point (b)(i), "organisation and personnel", requires the safety management system to address four linked items: the roles and responsibilities of personnel involved in the management of major hazards at all levels, measures to raise awareness of the need for continuous improvement, "the identification of training needs of such personnel and the provision of the training so identified", and the involvement of employees and of subcontracted personnel working in the establishment who are important from the point of view of safety.

The wording sets a two step process: a documented training needs analysis for major hazard roles, then delivery of exactly what that analysis identifies. An operator that delivers courses without a traceable needs analysis cannot show the second step follows from the first. The method is described in [how to conduct a training needs analysis](/guides/how-to-conduct-a-training-needs-analysis).

Annex III, point (a), adds that the system "shall be proportionate to the hazards, industrial activities and complexity of the organisation in the establishment and be based on assessment of the risks". A small lower tier warehouse and a large upper tier refinery therefore need different training depth, but both need the needs analysis.

sections.heading: What emergency training does Seveso III require?

blocks.text: Annex III, point (b)(v), "planning for emergencies", requires procedures to identify foreseeable emergencies by systematic analysis, to prepare, test and review emergency plans, and "to provide specific training for the staff concerned". It then states: "Such training shall be given to all personnel working in the establishment, including relevant subcontracted personnel."

For upper tier establishments, Article 12 adds the internal emergency plan. Article 12(4) requires the plan to be drawn up in consultation with the personnel working inside the establishment, including long term relevant subcontracted personnel, and Article 12(6) requires it to be reviewed, tested and where necessary updated at intervals of no longer than three years. Annex IV, point 1(f) requires the internal plan to include, where necessary, "arrangements for training staff in the duties they will be expected to perform" and coordination with off site emergency services.

blocks.title: The three year test cycle is a training input
blocks.text: Article 12(6) is one of the few hard intervals in Seveso III. Each test of the internal emergency plan shows whether staff can perform their assigned duties, and the findings should feed the next round of emergency training.

sections.heading: Which other safety management elements depend on trained people?

blocks.text: Several other Annex III elements assume competent people and need their own training content. Training owners should treat them as distinct competence areas rather than one generic course.

items: **Identification and evaluation of major hazards (b)(ii):** procedures for systematically identifying hazards from normal and abnormal operation, including subcontracted activities, and assessing likelihood and severity.
**Operational control (b)(iii):** procedures and instructions for safe operation, including maintenance, alarm management, temporary stoppages, and management of ageing equipment and corrosion.
**Management of change (b)(iv):** procedures for planning modifications and designing new installations, processes or storage facilities.
**Monitoring performance (b)(vi):** reporting and investigating major accidents and near misses, particularly failures of protective measures, and follow up on lessons learned.
**Audit and review (b)(vii):** periodic systematic assessment of the policy and the safety management system, with documented review by senior management.

blocks.text: Management of change is the element most often linked to training failures: a modified process with unchanged training leaves operators applying outdated procedures. Linking each change record to a training impact check is a practical control, and it parallels the approach used for process safety in the United States described in [OSHA process safety management training requirements](/regulations/osha-process-safety-management-training-requirements).

sections.heading: Which obligations apply to which roles, and what evidence would an inspector expect?

blocks.text: Article 20(2) requires inspections to be sufficient for a planned and systematic examination of the technical, organizational and managerial systems at the establishment, so training evidence is examined as part of the safety management system. The table maps each obligation to its role, frequency, and evidence.

blocks.text: Article 20(4) sets the inspection rhythm: the period between two consecutive site visits must not exceed one year for upper tier and three years for lower tier establishments, unless the competent authority has drawn up a program based on a systematic appraisal of hazards. Records therefore need to be audit ready continuously, as covered in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How do the duties differ between lower tier and upper tier sites?

blocks.text: Both tiers must write a major accident prevention policy (MAPP) and implement it, but upper tier sites carry heavier documentation and emergency planning duties. Article 8(5) allows lower tier establishments to implement the MAPP "by other appropriate means, structures and management systems", proportionate to the hazards and taking into account the Annex III principles.

Upper tier operators must also produce a safety report under Article 10, demonstrating that a MAPP and a safety management system have been put into effect in line with Annex III, and an internal emergency plan under Article 12. The Annex III training principles therefore apply to both tiers, but only upper tier sites must evidence them in a formal safety report. Sites that also have zoned areas should coordinate with [ATEX workplace training](/regulations/eu-atex-workplace-directive-training), and the sector context is on the [energy and resources industry page](/industries/energy-resources).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models major accident scenarios, the controls that prevent them, and the roles responsible for each control as linked concepts with assessment points. That structure makes the Annex III training needs analysis traceable to specific hazards, and it shows which roles need retraining when a management of change record or an emergency plan test alters a control.

faqs.q: Does Seveso III set a training frequency?
faqs.a: Not for training as such. It requires the safety management system to identify and meet training needs and to train all personnel for emergencies. The fixed intervals it sets are for testing internal emergency plans (no longer than three years) and reviewing the MAPP and safety report (at least every five years).

faqs.q: Do contractors need Seveso emergency training?
faqs.a: Yes, where relevant. Annex III, point (b)(v) states that emergency training shall be given to all personnel working in the establishment, including relevant subcontracted personnel. Article 12(4) also requires consultation with long term relevant subcontracted personnel when drawing up the internal emergency plan.

faqs.q: Does Seveso III apply to lower tier sites' training?
faqs.a: Yes. Lower tier operators must implement their MAPP by appropriate means proportionate to the hazards, taking into account the Annex III principles, which include identifying and providing training. They are not required to produce a safety report or an internal emergency plan under the directive.

faqs.q: Is Seveso III enforced by labor inspectors?
faqs.a: It is enforced by the competent authorities each Member State designates for major accident hazards, which may be environmental, civil protection, or labor bodies depending on the country. Article 20 requires them to run a system of inspections covering all establishments.
